National Consumer Disputes Redressal
Nagpur Agriculture Equipment ... vs Premnath on 2 July, 2020
NATIONAL CONSUMER DISPUTES REDRESSAL COMMISSION NEW DELHI   REVISION PETITION NO. 342 OF 2015   (Against the Order dated 17/09/2014 in Appeal No. 629/2008 of the State Commission Maharashtra) 1. NAGPUR AGRICULTURE EQUIPMENT ENGINEERS PRIVATE LTD. & ANR. NAGPUR AGRICULTURE EQUIPMENT,
ENGINNEERS PVT LTD.,
74-A CENTRAL AVENUE, NAGPUR MAHARASHTRA 2. THE MANAGER/DIRECTOR, M/S SONALIKA AGRO INDUSTRIES CORPORATION, 6 INDUSTRIAL ESTATE,
JALANDHAR ROAD,
 HOSHIARPUR PUNJAB ...........Petitioner(s) Versus   1. PREMNATH S/O. VITTHALRAO PATIL,
R/O GUMGAON, HINGANA, NAGPUR MAHARASHTRA ...........Respondent(s) 
 BEFORE:     HON'BLE DR. S.M. KANTIKAR,PRESIDING MEMBER

 Pronounced on: 2nd July 2020

 ORDER
1. This Revision Petition has been filed under
Section 21(b)
of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, hereinafter referred to as the "Act 1986‟, challenging the Order dated 17.09.2014 passed by the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (for short "State Commission") in First Appeal No. A/629/08 arising out of the Order dated 09.06.2008 in C.C. No. 559 of 2007 passed by the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum, Nagpur, (for short, 'The District Forum") wherein the appeal was partly allowed.
2.       Briefly stated facts relevant for the disposal of this Petition, are that   the complainant Premnath purchased a Sonalika thresher machine from Nagpur Agriculture Equipment Engineers Private Ltd. (OP-1) for Rs. 1,02,500/-. The machine was manufactured by M/s Sonalika Agro Industries Corporation (OP-2). It was alleged that due to the throwing of dust from the feeding hole, the machine could not work efficiently. The thresher work could not be done. The complainant alleged that it was due to manufacturing defect in the machine. The OP-1 did not heed attention to the repeated complaints of the complainant. The complainant sustained a loss of his earnings at Rs. 3,000/- per day. Alleging deficiency in service on the part of the OPs the complainant filed a complaint before the District Forum, Nagpur seeking compensation and replacement of the machine.
3.       The OPs filed their respective replies and raised preliminary objection that the complainant was not a consumer; he purchased the machine for business purpose. The OP- 1 filed a civil suit against the complainant for recovery of unpaid price of the machine in question. The complainant has not filed any expert report to show that there was defect in the machine. The OPs denied any manufacturing defects in the thresher machine.
4.       The District Forum, after taking into account the averments of  the parties held that the complainant was using the machine for business purpose, thus not consumer and there was no expert report to prove defective machine and dismissed the complaint.
5.       The Complainants filed Appeal under
Section 15
of the Act before the State Commission. The Appeal was partly allowed by the State Commission with observation in its paras 10 and 11 as below:
10.   The complaint shows that the appellant does not have any land in his name, so as to support his livelihood. He has filed the 7/12, extract showing name of some other person. This shows that the purchase of machine was only to support his livelihood. It's a common experience that the persons from village always claim their profession to be farming though they may not have sufficient land which alone can sustain their livelihood so that any other extra profession can be termed as an extra commercial activity. Also the respondents have not produced any evidence to show that the appellant was dependent on another profession like farming and the thresher was purchased purely for commercial activity to earn profits. Thus, we see that the thresher was purchased only to earn livelihood by the appellant and can not be claimed to be an extra commercial activity so as to throw him out of the definition of Consumer. We feel the Forum erred in considering the livelihood activity to be the commercial activity.
11.  The major contention raised by the respondent in the absence of technical report regarding defect in the thresher machine. But as a consumer, the appellant has filed the complaint with his experience of working on the machine that , it was throwing dust through feeding hole thereby making difficult to feed the raw material for processing. The appellant's experienced difficulty in the functioning of the thresher. It then becomes the responsibility of the manufacturer and the seller i.e respondent Nos. 1&2 to give the reasons for the same and remove said defect. We do not find any cogent explanation, evidence or reason, to disbelieve the case of the appellant while operating it. Hence we find no necessity of any specific technical certification by any expert on behalf of appellant to show the defect in the machine. It also becomes incumbent, upon the respondent Nos. 1 & 2 to repair the machine and provide satisfactory service to the purchaser- consumer. The respondents do not appear to have done it, but the respondent No. 1 has resorted to file a counter case to add tangent, to the complaint of the consumer and deny him the service. We therefore hold that, the complaint of the appellant is justifiable and the respondents are bound to repair the machine or compensate it as fair trade practice.
(paras 10 and 11  from order of State Commission)

 

The State Commission vide its order dated 17.09.2014 and directed the OPs to pay Rs. 1,02,500/- jointly and severally with interest @ 9 % from 01.10.2007 (date of purchase), OP-1 to pay to the complainant Rs. 5,000/- as compensation for mental and physical torture and Rs. 3,000/- towards the cost. It was further directed to the OPs to pay jointly and severally Rs. 100/- per day as loss of earning from the date of purchase till the date of payment.
6.       Being aggrieved the OPs filed the instant Revision Petition before this Commission.
7.       Heard the learned counsel for both the sides. The complainant was present during argument with his Counsel. Perused the material on record. Original record from the District Forum was requisitioned.
8.       Learned Counsel for the complainant argued that he noticed a defect within two months of purchase of the Sonalika thrasher machine. It was throwing dust from the same hole / entrance from which the food grains are pushed in the machine. Therefore it was impossible to stand near the inlet and impossible to push continuously the food grains material. The complainant immediately approached to the OP-1 for the said defect.   The OP-1 sent a mechanic for seven times within two months, but the defect was not cured. Even the Complainant with the help of four villagers took the machine for repairs to the OP-1 workshop at Mandhal Tq. Kuhi but machine was not repaired. The complainant was facing hardship and suffered heavy financial loss from the date of purchase of the machine.
9.       The learned counsel for OPs submitted that the complainant suppressed the use of thrasher machine for commercial purpose. Thus, he was not a Consumer under the Act, 1986. The complaint being afflictive in nature and it was to be adjudicated only in a Civil Court. Before purchase of Sonalika thrasher machine the complainant was shown other machines. The complainant with his previous experience gone through the brochures, done comparative evaluation of all products, and decided to purchase the said thrasher. The Sonalika thrasher machine was ISI marked with certified International quality. It was installed by an expert having no manufacturing defect.
10.     The main thrust of the argument from the learned counsel for the petitioners that the onus to prove there was manufacturing defect in the thrasher was upon the complainant and the complaint failed to produce any expert report.  I would like to place reliance upon the view taken by this Commission in RP No. 381 of 2012 decided on 17.10.2014/05.11.2014, "Ankur Seeds Private Limited & Anr. vs Moti Lal & Anr.", which has been stated as below:
"It is cardinal principle of law that ordinarily the burden of proving the fact rests on the party who asserts the affirmative issues and not on the party who denies it. Nevertheless, there is distinction between the phrase burden of proof and onus of proof. Explaining the said distinction, in
A. Raghavamma & Anr. Vs. A. Chenchamma & Anr.
AIR 1964 SC 136, a three-Judge Bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that: there is essential distinction between burden of proof and onus of proof: burden of proof lies on the person who has to prove a fact and it never shifts, but the onus of proof shifts. Such a shifting of onus is a continuous process in the evaluation of evidence."
In my view therefore, to give effect to the Objective of the Act, its provisions have to be construed by resorting to the Doctrine of 'Purposive Construction'. Considered from that perspective, in my opinion, if a Complainant is able to create a high degree of probability of deficiency on the part of the Opposite Party, the onus would shift on to the Opposite Party (the defendant) to discharge the onus to prove his denial."
11.     The manufacturer as well as the supplier has a duty to exercise due care and caution in providing a product/ machine which is fit for the purpose for which it is sold. Throwing of dust from the feeding hole, in it shows that there is manufacturing defect in the machine and no need to prove it. Thus, the technical certification was not absolute in this case.
12.     I see, there is no such concept of goods suffering from manufacturing defect enshrined by the provision of the Act,1986, it only defines the word defect by way of
Section 2(1) (f)
which is to the following effect:
"Defect" means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied, or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods.
Thus in my view, it is a misconceived notion that any machine or vehicle for that purpose any goods can be ordered to be replaced or the cost can be ordered to be refunded only if they suffer from manufacturing defect.
13.     Generally, whenever a consumer goes for brand new goods like a thrasher in this case has minimum expectation that he would not encounter or face any inconvenience or hardship for few months or a year or within warranty.  In case if he had to take the machine  time and again to the workshop or call the technician time and again for removing one defect or the other, certainly he suffers immensely loss of time, loss of business, physical discomfort and emotional sufferings for purchasing such new machine by paying heavy amount.
14.      I find, the defect in thrasher in the instant case continues for months together and erupts time and again, thus no other inference can be drawn than that the machine suffers from manufacturing defect as defect which is not of manufacturing nature can be rectified or removed without its recurrence or without giving any further inconvenience to the consumer.
15.     My view is that the onus shifts to the manufacturer to show that the machine  does not suffer from manufacturing defect once complainant has proved and discharged the initial onus that the machine was defective on    showing that machine was attended for many occasion (seven times) for removing one defect.  It is pertinent to note that the thrasher machine was taken to OP's workshop with the help of four people is sufficient to draw the inference that the machine was a defective one.
16.     For such type of manufacturers and service providers the Hon'ble Supreme court has in
Ghaziabad Development Authority Vs. Balbir Singh
(2004) 5 Supreme Court Cases 65 come down heavily and called upon the Consumer Forum and Commissions established under the Act, 1986 to not only compensate the consumer as to the actual loss suffered by him but also to compensate him as to the mental agony, harassment, emotional suffering, physical discomfort, loss of business, loss of time by taking vehicle time and again to the workshop.
17.     Based on the discussion above and considering that the machine purchased in 2007 has already become very old and the complainant suffered loss and agony for more than one decade, I do not find any illegality, irregularity or jurisdictional error in the order passed by the State Commission. Accordingly, the said order is upheld and the Revision Petition, being without any merit, is dismissed, as there does not seem to be any sufficient ground to interfere in the exercise of the revisional jurisdiction by this Commission.
There shall be no order as to costs.
...................... DR. S.M. KANTIKAR PRESIDING MEMBER
